Our editorial process produces two outputs: (i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; (ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Neural entrainment is strongest to the spectral flux of slow music and depends on familiarity and beat salience" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and Barbara Shinn-Cunningham as the Senior Editor. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Benedikt Zoefel (Reviewer #1) and Nate Zuk (Reviewer #3).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

In general the reviewers were positive however more work needs to be done to validate that the results are not a consequence of the analyses or the specific choice of music before tempo manipulation as pointed out by the reviewers. Also, it would be important to better clarify the concepts of neural entertainment, synchronization and neural tracking and their meaning in this specific context.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

I believe the authors could emphasize their most important results more when they appear in the Results section. An example is the beginning of page 11 where one important sentence ("SRCoh was highest…") is hidden in the text. This result is interesting – highlighting it would also make main results easier to extract.

RCA: "These approaches have been criticized because of their potential susceptibility to autocorrelation". As the authors mention a possible involvement of neural oscillations (in their introduction), it could be useful to point out that a removal of autocorrelation (to calculate TRF) might actually remove oscillations as well.

Due to differences in x and y axes, I was initially confused by Figure 1c, wondering why stimulation tempo (Hz) does not correspond to FFT frequency (Hz). Maybe the authors could include lines to show where stimulation tempo = FFT frequency and the first harmonic? This would make the relevant information much easier to extract.

I leave it to the authors, but an additional point that might be worth discussing is the fact that humans seem to be most sensitive to amplitude modulations at higher frequencies (around 4 Hz) than those that seem to play an important role in the current study (1-2 Hz). This is for example summarized in a review by Edwards and Chang (2013, Hear Res). Other relevant work is that by Teng, Poeppel and colleagues showing theta activity to most reliably follow acoustic rhythms. Could the authors discuss whether this means that music is special or other reasons for relatively low preferred rates in their work?

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

The paper was very nice but sometimes hard to read because I am not so confident with the difference between engagement, entertainment, synchronization and tracking. In the literature, those terms are sometimes used interchangeably, and sometimes instead, they are used with a precise meaning. I suggest the authors think about rephrasing parts of the paper and clarifying those terms from the beginning to broaden the range of readers that can enjoy the paper in depth. I found very few typos, and the visualizations were nice. Sometimes I think that the plots are too small and hard to read, and the x/y axes proportion must be chosen carefully.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

p. 4, line 72: "…and we are not aware…tempo-modulated". I think Kaneshiro et al., 2020 fits this description. They did not use a controlled spacing of tempos like was done in this study, but they used naturalistic polyphonic music with a variety of tempos. Rajendran et al., 2020 also fits this description, although they did extracellular recordings and not EEG.

p. 6, line 106-107: "…spectral flux is sensitive…changes in amplitude." Can you provide a citation where rhythmic information is provided by changes in pitch but not in amplitude, perhaps including a behavioral measure of rhythm salience?

Figure 1C: I think the reason the z-scored amplitude decreases with decreasing stimulation tempo is because z-scoring reduces the magnitude of the components as more non-zero spectral components are introduced in the range of interest. This could be confusing to readers given that EEG may track these tempos better. The authors could alternatively z-score the original signals (before computing the spectra), which might result in more consistent amplitudes across stimulation tempo.

p. 20, lines 368-370: "In this study…tapped frequency." I think this should go earlier in the results, around where Figure 1 is presented, in order to clarify the difference between "stimulation tempo" (which is referred to earlier) and "tapped beat rate".

p. 25-26, lines 481-510: This discussion aims to highlight the importance of considering other stimulus features besides the envelope (like spectral flux) when comparing the neural tracking of speech and music, partly via criticizing Zuk et al. (2021) for focusing on the envelope. However, the current study does not fully back up some of the author's critiques, mainly because speech stimuli were not included in this study. We don't know how much spectral flux improves EEG prediction of speech over envelope-based measures, although it likely will (see the use of spectrotemporal changes and acoustic edges in Daube et al., 2019). But we can instead compare the prediction accuracies to Di Liberto et al., 2015, Current Biology.

Envelope-based forward modeling of speech produces the worst average prediction accuracies around 0.05, and the accuracies increase as features such as the spectrogram and phonetic features are added (Figure 2 of that paper). These prediction accuracies are above the prediction accuracies in the current study (0.04 on average with spectral flux, and 0.06 for the slowest tempos, see Figure 3 of this study), supporting the possibility that speech is generally tracked better than music. I agree it is possible that other musical features may predict EEG better and could produce comparable prediction accuracies to speech. But for the discussion here, the authors should instead focus on how similarities and differences in relevant features for speech and music could affect interpretations for studies comparing neural tracking, which would nicely follow the first paragraph of this section. More specifically, the authors should clarify what "characterize stimuli as fairly as possible" (line 509) means and suggest alternative ways of comparing speech and music. If they choose to criticize studies using the envelope alone (which might not be necessary to make their point), I recommend also acknowledging that their study does not directly address questions about speech and music comparisons and that more work needs to be done to understand the differences between speech and music tracking.

p. 25, lines 497-498: "…we found…envelope." It is not clear if spectral flux causes stronger entrainment given the data. Rephrase to: "…we found that spectral flux was tracked better than the amplitude envelope."

p. 26, lines 520-521: "…and ease of beat tapping…stimulation tempi." The statistical analysis of the data in Figure 3 showed that ease of beat tapping did not significantly vary with stimulation tempo (lines 327-329), which contradicts this statement.

p. 28, lines 532-535: "One is that our study…entrainment." I don't understand why this would matter, because the analysis was done after selecting "musical" and "non-musical" subjects. Perhaps cut this?

p. 29, line 594: "correlate" should be "correlated".

p. 32, line 647-648: "Each segment…0.25 Hz." The details for the range of tempi are in Supplementary Table 1, but it would be useful here to state the maximum amount of tempo shift relative to the original, both for increasing and decreasing the tempo. Additionally, I mentioned in the public review that the original tempos seem to span the range with the best neural tracking. You should also state the original range of tempos here.

p. 34, lines 703-704: "This signal…AFz position." Why did you choose to reference this way? Is there a related citation?

p. 37, line 773: "To statistically asses" should be "assess".

p. 40, section EEG – Reliable Components Analysis, Temporal Response Function: In the public review, I suggested normalizing the measures of correlation, coherence, and prediction accuracy by null distributions. When you do so, make sure the shuffling of trials is done using trials with the same tempi. Otherwise, there will be a mismatch in the spectral content of the music due to differences in tempi, which defeats the point of generating the null distributions.

p. 40, line 855: "…a system identification technique…" This isn't quite true, change to "…a modeling technique…".

p. 41, lines 873-884, also Figure 3C: From my understanding, TRFs were fit to each stimulus feature separately. I am ok with this for comparing prediction accuracies because the models appear to have the same dimensionality (T x 1, where T is the number of lags). However, this is potentially an issue for interpreting TRF weights because the stimulus features in the separate models are correlated, so peaks and troughs found in the TRF for one model might be the effect of one of the other features. One possibility is to look at the TRF weights of the full model instead, but ridge unfortunately optimizes the model by making the weights correlated (an effect that produces smooth TRFs), so I don't think it alleviates the issue either. The best approach would be to iteratively partial out the contribution of each stimulus feature. Start with the envelope model, compute the EEG prediction with that model, and then subtract the prediction from the EEG data. Then fit the derivative model and then the beats model, removing each after they are fit. This way, the TRF weights found for the spectral flux model reflect the temporal response after removing the effects of the other stimulus features.

p. 42-43, lines 903-933: In the public review, I mentioned that the TRF-SVM modeling needed to be clearer. Specifically:

– How are the TRFs fit for each group? If you are using a leave-one-trial-out procedure like before, the resulting TRFs for each trial are the models fit to all trials except the testing trial. As a result, they are going to be highly similar to each other, which could explain why the SVM performs so well. Here, I recommend instead fitting the TRF to each trial separately (no cross-validation) using the same ridge parameter that you found for the model trained earlier (in the section EEG – Temporal Response Function). That way the TRFs will represent the stimulus-response mappings for each individual trial.

– Clarify which training step was referred to for calculating the surrogate data (line 920). I recommend shuffling prior to the TRF modeling step, although if you fit the TRF to each trial individually then the result of shuffling before vs after will be the same.

– Lines 913-916: There are 6 trials at tapped rate, and 6 trials at 2x tapped rate, which should result in n=12 not n=13.

Figure 5 – supplement 1: The distributions on the left don't look like they come from the points on the right in each plot. Can you check if there was a mistake with the points plotted or the y-axes?

claims.source: Independent of whether the analysis approach was based on temporal response functions (TRFs) or reliable components analysis (RCA), the spectral flux of music – as opposed to the amplitude envelope – evoked strongest neural synchronization.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from both TRF and RCA analyses.

claims.claim: Music with slower beat rates elicited the strongest neural response.
claims.source: Moreover, music with slower beat rates, high familiarity, and easy-to-perceive beats elicited the strongest neural response.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental measurements across tempo conditions.

claims.claim: Music with high familiarity elicited the strongest neural response.
claims.source: Moreover, music with slower beat rates, high familiarity, and easy-to-perceive beats elicited the strongest neural response.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing familiar vs. unfamiliar music.

claims.claim: Music with easy-to-perceive beats elicited the strongest neural response.
claims.source: Moreover, music with slower beat rates, high familiarity, and easy-to-perceive beats elicited the strongest neural response.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing subjective ratings of beat perception ease.

claims.claim: Neural activity synchronizes to different types of rhythmic sounds, such as speech and music.
claims.source: Neural activity synchronizes to different types of rhythmic sounds, such as speech and music (Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Nicolaou et al., 2017; Ding et al., 2017; Kösem et al., 2018) over a wide range of rates.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: In music, neural activity synchronizes with the beat.
claims.source: In music, neural activity synchronizes with the beat, the most prominent isochronous pulse in music to which listeners sway their bodies or tap their feet (Tierney and Kraus, 2015; Nozaradan et al., 2012; Large and Snyder, 2009; Doelling and Poeppel, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The beat is the most prominent isochronous pulse in music to which listeners sway their bodies or tap their feet.
claims.source: In music, neural activity synchronizes with the beat, the most prominent isochronous pulse in music to which listeners sway their bodies or tap their feet (Tierney and Kraus, 2015; Nozaradan et al., 2012; Large and Snyder, 2009; Doelling and Poeppel, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a definition supported by cited literature and general knowledge in music perception.

claims.claim: Listeners show a strong behavioral preference for music with beat rates around 2 Hz.
claims.source: Listeners show a strong behavioral preference for music with beat rates around 2 Hz (here, we use the term tempo to refer to the beat rate).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the broader literature context and is consistent with the study's findings.

claims.claim: The preference for 2 Hz coincides with the modal tempo of Western pop music.
claims.source: The preference for 2 Hz coincides with the modal tempo of Western pop music (Moelants, 2002) and the most prominent frequency of natural adult body movements (MacDougall and Moore, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The preference for 2 Hz coincides with the most prominent frequency of natural adult body movements.
claims.source: The preference for 2 Hz coincides with the modal tempo of Western pop music (Moelants, 2002) and the most prominent frequency of natural adult body movements (MacDougall and Moore, 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Listeners perceive rhythmic sequences at beat rates around 1–2 Hz especially accurately when they are able to track the beat by moving their bodies.
claims.source: Indeed, previous research showed that listeners perceive rhythmic sequences at beat rates around 1–2 Hz especially accurately when they are able to track the beat by moving their bodies (Zalta et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Studies looking at tempo-dependence of neural synchronization are scarce.
claims.source: Despite the perceptual and motor evidence, studies looking at tempo-dependence of neural synchronization are scarce (Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Nicolaou et al., 2017) and we are not aware of any human EEG study using naturalistic polyphonic musical stimuli that were manipulated in the tempo domain.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature supported by limited citations.

claims.claim: There are no human EEG studies using naturalistic polyphonic musical stimuli that were manipulated in the tempo domain.
claims.source: Despite the perceptual and motor evidence, studies looking at tempo-dependence of neural synchronization are scarce (Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Nicolaou et al., 2017) and we are not aware of any human EEG study using naturalistic polyphonic musical stimuli that were manipulated in the tempo domain.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature based on the authors' knowledge.

claims.claim: A number of different musical, behavioral, and perceptual measures have been shown to modulate neural synchronization and influence music perception, including complexity, familiarity, repetition of the music, musical training of the listener, and attention to the stimulus.
claims.source: In addition, a number of different musical, behavioral, and perceptual measures have been shown to modulate neural synchronization and influence music perception, including complexity, familiarity, repetition of the music, musical training of the listener, and attention to the stimulus (Kumagai et al., 2018; Madsen et al., 2019; Doelling and Poeppel, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: Most studies assessing neural synchronization to music have examined synchronization to either the stimulus amplitude envelope or 'higher order' musical features such as surprise and expectation.
claims.source: Most studies assessing neural synchronization to music have examined synchronization to either the stimulus amplitude envelope, which quantifies intensity fluctuations over time (Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Kaneshiro et al., 2020; Wollman et al., 2020), or 'higher order' musical features such as surprise and expectation (Di Liberto et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature supported by citations.

claims.claim: The amplitude envelope quantifies intensity fluctuations over time.
claims.source: Most studies assessing neural synchronization to music have examined synchronization to either the stimulus amplitude envelope, which quantifies intensity fluctuations over time (Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Kaneshiro et al., 2020; Wollman et al., 2020), or 'higher order' musical features such as surprise and expectation (Di Liberto et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a definition supported by general knowledge in signal processing.

claims.claim: Neural activity has been shown to synchronize with the amplitude envelope in speech.
claims.source: This mimics approaches used for studying neural synchronization to speech, where neural activity has been shown to synchronize with the amplitude envelope (Peelle and Davis, 2012), which roughly corresponds to syllabic fluctuations (Doelling et al., 2014), as well as to 'higher order' semantic information (Broderick et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The amplitude envelope in speech roughly corresponds to syllabic fluctuations.
claims.source: This mimics approaches used for studying neural synchronization to speech, where neural activity has been shown to synchronize with the amplitude envelope (Peelle and Davis, 2012), which roughly corresponds to syllabic fluctuations (Doelling et al., 2014), as well as to 'higher order' semantic information (Broderick et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Most studies that have examined neural synchronization to musical rhythm have used simplified musical stimuli.
claims.source: Notably, most studies that have examined neural synchronization to musical rhythm have used simplified musical stimuli, such as MIDI melodies (Kumagai et al., 2018) and monophonic melodies (Di Liberto et al., 2020), or rhythmic lines comprising clicks or sine tones (Nozaradan et al., 2012; Nozaradan et al., 2011; Wollman et al., 2020); only a few studies have focused on naturalistic, polyphonic music (Tierney and Kraus, 2015; Madsen et al., 2019; Kaneshiro et al., 2020; Doelling and Poeppel, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature supported by citations.

claims.claim: Only a few studies have focused on naturalistic, polyphonic music for neural synchronization research.
claims.source: Notably, most studies that have examined neural synchronization to musical rhythm have used simplified musical stimuli, such as MIDI melodies (Kumagai et al., 2018) and monophonic melodies (Di Liberto et al., 2020), or rhythmic lines comprising clicks or sine tones (Nozaradan et al., 2012; Nozaradan et al., 2011; Wollman et al., 2020); only a few studies have focused on naturalistic, polyphonic music (Tierney and Kraus, 2015; Madsen et al., 2019; Kaneshiro et al., 2020; Doelling and Poeppel, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature supported by citations.

claims.claim: Neural activity synchronizes to amplitude fluctuations in music between 1 Hz and 8 Hz.
claims.source: 'Higher order' musical features are difficult to compute for naturalistic music, which is typically polyphonic and has complex spectro-temporal properties (Zatorre et al., 2002). However, amplitude-envelope synchronization is well documented: neural activity synchronizes to amplitude fluctuations in music between 1 Hz and 8 Hz, and synchronization is especially strong for listeners with musical expertise (Doelling and Poeppel, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Synchronization to amplitude fluctuations in music is especially strong for listeners with musical expertise.
claims.source: 'Higher order' musical features are difficult to compute for naturalistic music, which is typically polyphonic and has complex spectro-temporal properties (Zatorre et al., 2002). However, amplitude-envelope synchronization is well documented: neural activity synchronizes to amplitude fluctuations in music between 1 Hz and 8 Hz, and synchronization is especially strong for listeners with musical expertise (Doelling and Poeppel, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Amplitude envelope might not be the only or most dominant feature to which neural activity could synchronize in natural polyphonic music.
claims.source: Because of the complex nature of natural polyphonic music, we hypothesized that amplitude envelope might not be the only or most dominant feature to which neural activity could synchronize (Müller, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis stated by the authors based on reasoning about music complexity.

claims.claim: Spectral flux describes spectral changes of the signal on a frame-to-frame basis by computing the difference between the spectral vectors of subsequent frames.
claims.source: We examined amplitude envelope, the first derivative of the amplitude envelope (usually more sensitive to sound onsets than the amplitude envelope), beat times, and spectral flux, which describes spectral changes of the signal on a frame-to-frame basis by computing the difference between the spectral vectors of subsequent frames (Müller, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Spectral flux is sensitive to rhythmic information that is communicated by changes in pitch even when they are not accompanied by changes in amplitude.
claims.source: One potential advantage of spectral flux over the envelope or its derivative is that spectral flux is sensitive to rhythmic information that is communicated by changes in pitch even when they are not accompanied by changes in amplitude.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical advantage stated by the authors based on the properties of spectral flux.

claims.claim: Temporal and spectral information jointly influence the perceived accent structure in music, which provides information about beat locations.
claims.source: Critically, temporal and spectral information jointly influence the perceived accent structure in music, which provides information about beat locations (Pfordresher, 2003; Ellis and Jones, 2009; Jones, 1993).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: RCA-based analyses usually calculate correlation or coherence between a stimulus and relatively narrow-band activity.
claims.source: RCA-based analyses usually calculate correlation or coherence between a stimulus and relatively narrow-band activity, and in turn interpret neural synchronization as reflecting entrainment of a narrow-band neural oscillation to a stimulus rhythm (Doelling and Poeppel, 2015; Assaneo et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the RCA method supported by citations.

claims.claim: Spectral flux shared significant information with all other musical features.
claims.source: Spectral flux shared significant information with all other musical features; significant MI (relative to surrogate) was found between amplitude envelope and spectral flux (F(1,102)=24.68, pFDR = 1.01e-5, η2=0.18), derivative and spectral flux (F(1,102)=82.3, pFDR = 1.92e-13, η2=0.45) and beat times and spectral flux (F(1,102)=23.05, pFDR = 1.3e-5, η2=0.13).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the mutual information analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: There was significant shared information between the amplitude envelope and first derivative.
claims.source: Unsurprisingly, there was also significant shared information between the amplitude envelope and first derivative (F(1,102)=14.11, pFDR = 4.67e-4, η2=0.09); other comparisons: (Fenv-beat(1,102)=8.44, pFDR = 0.006, η2=0.07; Fder-beat(1,102)=6.06, pFDR = 0.016, η2=0.05).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the mutual information analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: The first reliable component exhibited an auditory topography.
claims.source: Our analyses focused on the first reliable component, which exhibited an auditory topography (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the RCA analysis supported by the topography shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Z-scored SRCorrs were significantly tempo-dependent for the amplitude envelope and the spectral flux.
claims.source: The resulting z-scored SRCorrs were significantly tempo-dependent for the amplitude envelope and the spectral flux (repeated-measure ANOVAs with Greenhouse-Geiser correction where required: Fenv(12,429)=2.5, pGG = 0.015, η2=0.07; Fder(12,429)=1.67, p=0.07, η2=0.05; Fbeat(12,429)=0.94, p=0.5, η2=0.03; Fspec(12,429)=2.92, pGG = 6.88e-4, η2=0.08).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the RCA analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: Highest correlations were found at slower tempi (~1–2 Hz).
claims.source: The resulting z-scored SRCorrs were significantly tempo-dependent for the amplitude envelope and the spectral flux (repeated-measure ANOVAs with Greenhouse-Geiser correction where required: Fenv(12,429)=2.5, pGG = 0.015, η2=0.07; Fder(12,429)=1.67, p=0.07, η2=0.05; Fbeat(12,429)=0.94, p=0.5, η2=0.03; Fspec(12,429)=2.92, pGG = 6.88e-4, η2=0.08). Highest correlations were found at slower tempi (~1–2 Hz).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the RCA analysis supported by the data.

claims.claim: SRCoh was stronger at the first harmonic of the stimulation tempo than at the stimulation tempo itself, regardless of the musical feature.
claims.source: Overall, SRCoh was stronger at the first harmonic of the stimulation tempo than at the stimulation tempo itself, regardless of the musical feature (Figure 2I, paired-sample t-test, envelope: t(12)=-5.16, pFDR = 0.001, re = 0.73; derivative: t(12)=-5.11, pFDR = 0.001, re = 0.72; beat: t(12)=-4.13, pFDR = 0.004, re = 0.64; spectral flux: t(12)=-3.3, pFDR = 0.01, re = 0.56).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the frequency-domain analysis supported by statistical tests and Figure 2I.

claims.claim: The stimuli themselves mostly also contained highest FFT amplitudes at the first harmonic.
claims.source: The stimuli themselves mostly also contained highest FFT amplitudes at the first harmonic (Figure 2J, envelope: t(12)=-6.81, pFDR = 5.23e-5, re=0.81; derivative: t(12)=-6.88, pFDR = 5.23e-5, re = 0.81; spectral flux: t(12)=-8.04, pFDR = 2.98e-5, re = 0.85), apart from the beat onsets (beat: t(12)=6.27, pFDR = 8.56–5. re = 0.79).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus analysis supported by statistical tests and Figure 2J.

claims.claim: Z-SRCoh was highest for slow music, but this tempo dependence was only significant for the spectral flux and beat onsets.
claims.source: Z-SRCoh was highest for slow music, but this tempo dependence was only significant for the spectral flux and beat onsets (Fenv(12,429)=1.31, p=0.21, η2=0.04; Fder(12,429)=1.71, p=0.06, η2=0.05; Fbeat(12,429)=2.07, pGG = 0.04, η2=0.06; Fspec(12,429)=2.82, pGG = 0.006, η2=0.08).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the frequency-domain analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: Significant effects of Tempo were observed for all musical features with z-TRF correlations being strongest at slower tempi (~1–2 Hz).
claims.source: After z-scoring the TRF correlations with respect to the surrogate distributions, as described for the SRcorr and SRcoh measures, repeated-measures ANOVAs showed that significant effects of Tempo were observed for all musical features with z-TRF correlations being strongest at slower tempi (~1–2 Hz) (Fenv(12,429)=2.47, p=0.004, η2=0.07; Fder(12,429)=1.84, pGG = 0.04, η2=0.05; Fbeat(12,429)=3.81, pGG = 3.18e-4, η2=0.11; Fspec(12,429)=12.87, pGG = 3.87e-13, η2=0.29).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the TRF analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: There was no significant effect on z-TRF correlations of how much music stimuli were tempo shifted.
claims.source: Thus, we conducted a control analysis to show that there was no significant effect on z-TRF correlations of how much music stimuli were tempo shifted (2.25 Hz: F(2,96)=0.45, P=0.43; 1.5 Hz: F(2,24)=0.49, p=0.49; Figure 3—figure supplement 3; for more details see Materials and methods).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis supported by statistical tests and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Strongest neural synchronization was found in response to spectral flux regardless of the dependent measure (RCA-SRCorr, RCA-SRCoh, TRF correlation).
claims.source: As natural music is a complex, multi-layered auditory stimulus, we sought to explore neural synchronization to different musical features and to identify the stimulus feature or features that would drive strongest neural synchronization. Regardless of the dependent measure (RCA-SRCorr, RCA-SRCoh, TRF correlation), strongest neural synchronization was found in response to spectral flux (Figures 2C, H, 3B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data from multiple analysis methods shown in Figures 2C, H, and 3B.

claims.claim: Significant differences were observed between the spectral flux and all other musical features based on z-scored SRCorr.
claims.source: In particular, significant differences (as quantified with a repeated-measure ANOVA followed by Tukey's test) were observed between the spectral flux and all other musical features based on z-scored SRCorr (FSRCorr(3,132)=39.27, pGG = 1.2e-16, η2=0.55), z-SRCoh (FSRCoh(3,132)=26.27, pGG = 1.72e-12, η2=0.45) and z-TRF correlations (FTRF(4,165)=30.09, pGG = 1.21e-13, η2=0.48).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from statistical comparisons of different musical features.

claims.claim: The spectral flux alone showed an advantage over the multi-featured TRF.
claims.source: Although there was a significant increase in z-TRF correlations in comparison to the amplitude envelope (repeated-measure ANOVA with follow-up Tukey's test, pFDR = 1.66e-08), first derivative (pFDR = 1.66e-8), and beat onsets (pFDR = 1.66e-8), the spectral flux alone showed an advantage over the multi-featured TRF (pFDR = 6.74e-8).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the multivariate TRF analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: Taking all stimulus features together is not a better descriptor of the neural response than the spectral flux alone.
claims.source: Thus, taking all stimulus features together is not a better descriptor of the neural response than the spectral flux alone, indicating together with the MI results from Figure 1 that spectral flux is a more complete representation of the rhythmic structure of the music than the other musical features.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multivariate TRF analysis and mutual information results.

claims.claim: Spectral flux is a more complete representation of the rhythmic structure of the music than the other musical features.
claims.source: Thus, taking all stimulus features together is not a better descriptor of the neural response than the spectral flux alone, indicating together with the MI results from Figure 1 that spectral flux is a more complete representation of the rhythmic structure of the music than the other musical features.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multivariate TRF analysis and mutual information results.

claims.claim: Linear slopes were significantly higher for spectral flux and the multivariate model compared to the remaining three musical features.
claims.source: Linear slopes were significantly higher for spectral flux and the multivariate model compared to the remaining three musical features (repeated-measure ANOVA with follow-up Tukey's test, envelope-spectral flux: pFDR = 2.8e-6; envelope – all: pFDR = 2.88e-4; derivative-spectral flux: pFDR = 7.47e-8; derivative – all: pFDR = 2.8e-6; beat-spectral flux: pFDR = 2.47e-8; beat – all: pFDR = 2.09e-5; spectral flux – all: pFDR = 0.01).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the slope comparison analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: Significant effects of tempo on TRF weights were observed for spectral flux between 102–211ms.
claims.source: Significant effects of tempo on TRF weights were observed for spectral flux between 102–211ms (p=0.01; Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the cluster-based permutation testing supported by Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The tempo specificity was observable in the amplitudes of the TRF weights, which were largest for slower music.
claims.source: The tempo specificity was observable in the amplitudes of the TRF weights, which were largest for slower music (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the TRF weight analysis supported by Figure 3F.

claims.claim: For all four musical features, SRCorr significantly predicted TRF correlations.
claims.source: For all four musical features, SRCorr significantly predicted TRF correlations (tenv(440) = 9.77, βenv=0.53, pFDR <1e-15, R2=0.51; tder(440) = 8.09, βder=0.46, pFDR = 5.77e-14, R2=0.28; tbeat(440) = 12.12, βbeat=0.67, pFDR <1e-15, R2=0.61; tspec(440) = 12.49, βspec=0.56, pFDR = 1e-15, R2=0.76).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the linear mixed-effects model analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: The strongest correlations between neural synchronization measures were found for the beat onsets and spectral flux of music.
claims.source: The strongest correlations between neural synchronization measures were found for the beat onsets and spectral flux of music (Figure 4C and D).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of TRF and RCA measures supported by Figures 4C and D.

claims.claim: For all musical features, the first harmonic was a better predictor of TRF correlations than the intended stimulation tempo except for the beat onsets.
claims.source: For all musical features, the first harmonic was a better predictor of TRF correlations than the intended stimulation tempo except for the beat onsets (intended tempo: tenv(440) = 4.78, βenv=0.17, pFDR = 3.15e-6, R2=0.34; tder(440) = 3.06, βder=0.1, pFDR = 0.002, R2=0.13; tbeat(440) = 8.12, βbeat=0.28, pFDR = 1.95e-14, R2=0.5; tspec(440) = 3.42, βspec=0.09, pFDR = 7.9e-4, R2=0.64; first harmonic: tenv(440) = 6.17, βenv=0.09, pFDR = 3.07e-9, R2=0.33; tder(440) = 4.98, βder=0.09, pFDR = 1.43e-6, R2=0.16; tbeat(440) = 8.79, βbeat=0.2, pFDR <1e-15, R2=0.51; tspec(440) = 6.87, βspec=0.09, pFDR = 5.82e-11, R2=0.64).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the linear mixed-effects model analysis comparing stimulation tempo and first harmonic.

claims.claim: TRF and RCA–SRCorr/RCA-SRCoh seem to pick up on similar features of the neural response.
claims.source: Overall, these results suggest that, despite their analytical differences as well as common differences in interpretation, TRF and RCA–SRCorr/RCA-SRCoh seem to pick up on similar features of the neural response, but may potentially strengthen each other's explanatory power when used together.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of TRF and RCA measures.

claims.claim: All behavioral ratings were unaffected by tempo.
claims.source: To evaluate the effects of tempo on the individuals' ratings, separate repeated-measure ANOVAs were conducted for each behavioral rating. All behavioral ratings were unaffected by tempo (enjoyment: F(12,429)=0.58, p=0.85, η2=0.02; familiarity: F(12,429)=1.44, pGG = 0.18, η2=0.04; ease of beat tapping: F(12,429)=1.62, P=0.08, η2=0.05).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral rating analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: TRF correlations were not significantly different for less enjoyed compared to more enjoyed music.
claims.source: TRF correlations were not significantly different for less enjoyed compared to more enjoyed music (paired-sample t-test, t(33)=1.91, pFDR = 0.06, re = 0.36; Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral rating analysis supported by statistical tests and Figure 5C.

claims.claim: Significantly higher TRF correlations were observed for familiar vs. unfamiliar songs.
claims.source: In contrast, significantly higher TRF correlations were observed for familiar vs. unfamiliar songs (t(33)=-2.57, pFDR = 0.03, re = 0.46), and for songs with an easier-to-perceive beat (t(33)=-2.43, pFDR = 0.03, re = 0.44).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral rating analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: Significantly higher TRF correlations were observed for songs with an easier-to-perceive beat.
claims.source: In contrast, significantly higher TRF correlations were observed for familiar vs. unfamiliar songs (t(33)=-2.57, pFDR = 0.03, re = 0.46), and for songs with an easier-to-perceive beat (t(33)=-2.43, pFDR = 0.03, re = 0.44).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral rating analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: Pairwise comparisons revealed higher stimulus-related FFT peaks for more enjoyed music.
claims.source: Pairwise comparisons revealed higher stimulus-related FFT peaks for more enjoyed music (t-test, t(33)=-2.79, pFDR = 0.01, re = 0.49), less familiar music (t(33)=2.73, pFDR = 0.01, re = 0.49) and easier-to-perceive beats (t(33)=-3.33, pFDR = 0.01, re = 0.56).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus FFT analysis supported by statistical tests.

claims.claim: No significant correlations were observed between musical sophistication and TRF correlations.
claims.source: No significant correlations were observed between musical sophistication and TRF correlations (Pearson correlation, envelope: R=−0.21, pFDR = 0.32; derivative: R=−0.24, pFDR = 0.31; beats: R=−0.04, pFDR = 0.81; spectral flux: R=−0.34, pFDR = 0.2; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the musical sophistication analysis supported by statistical tests and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Strongest neural synchronization was found in response to stimulation tempi between 1 and 2 Hz in terms of SRCorr, TRF correlations, and TRF weights.
claims.source: Strongest neural synchronization was found in response to stimulation tempi between 1 and 2 Hz in terms of SRCorr (Figure 2B), TRF correlations (Figure 3A), and TRF weights (Figure 3C–F).
claims.evidence: This is a summary finding supported by data from multiple analyses shown in Figures 2B, 3A, and 3C-F.

claims.claim: The group preference for music tapping was at 1.55 Hz.
claims.source: Moreover, we observed a behavioral preference to tap to the beat in this frequency range, as the group preference for music tapping was at 1.55 Hz (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the behavioral tapping analysis supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Previous studies have shown a preference to listen to music with beat rates around 2 Hz.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown a preference to listen to music with beat rates around 2 Hz (Bauer et al., 2015), which is moreover the modal beat rate in Western pop music (Moelants, 2002) and the rate at which the modulation spectrum of natural music peaks (Ding et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: 2 Hz is the modal beat rate in Western pop music.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown a preference to listen to music with beat rates around 2 Hz (Bauer et al., 2015), which is moreover the modal beat rate in Western pop music (Moelants, 2002) and the rate at which the modulation spectrum of natural music peaks (Ding et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: 2 Hz is the rate at which the modulation spectrum of natural music peaks.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown a preference to listen to music with beat rates around 2 Hz (Bauer et al., 2015), which is moreover the modal beat rate in Western pop music (Moelants, 2002) and the rate at which the modulation spectrum of natural music peaks (Ding et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: When asked to rhythmically move their bodies at a comfortable rate, adults will spontaneously move at rates around 2 Hz.
claims.source: Moreover, when asked to rhythmically move their bodies at a comfortable rate, adults will spontaneously move at rates around 2 Hz (McAuley et al., 2006) regardless whether they use their hands or feet (Rose et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: There is a tight link between preferred rates of human body movement and preferred rates for the music we make and listen to.
claims.source: Thus, there is a tight link between preferred rates of human body movement and preferred rates for the music we make and listen to that was moreover reflected in our neural data.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the literature and the study's findings.

results.result: Spectral flux of music evoked the strongest neural synchronization compared to amplitude envelope, first derivative, and beat onsets, across both TRF and RCA analysis methods. This superiority held even when compared to a multivariate model combining all other features, suggesting spectral flux captures more complete rhythmic information.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C41-C45 demonstrate consistent findings across multiple analysis approaches (TRF and RCA) with statistical support (C42: p<1e-12 to 1e-16). The mutual information analysis (C31) and multivariate TRF results (C43, C91-C92) provide converging evidence. However, the control for autocorrelation differences between methods and potential confounds from stimulus feature correlations could be more thoroughly addressed.

results.result: Neural synchronization was strongest for music with slower beat rates (1-2 Hz), demonstrated through tempo-dependent effects in SRCorr, SRCoh, TRF correlations, and TRF weights. This tempo preference was most pronounced for spectral flux.
results.evaluation: Multiple converging measures (C34-C35, C38-C39, C59) show consistent tempo effects with statistical support. The control analysis (C40, C71) addresses potential confounds from tempo manipulation magnitude. The findings align with behavioral tapping preferences (C60: 1.55 Hz) and prior literature (C61-C64), strengthening the interpretation. Effect sizes are modest (η²=0.07-0.29) but consistent.

results.result: Music with high familiarity elicited stronger neural synchronization as measured by TRF correlations, consistent with prior research showing enhanced neural responses to familiar music.
results.evaluation: The finding is supported by statistical tests (C55: t(33)=-2.57, pFDR=0.03, re=0.46) and aligns with cited prior work (C100). However, the analysis is based on only 15 highest vs. 15 lowest rated trials per participant, which is a relatively small subset. The stimulus FFT analysis (C57) reveals a confound: less familiar music had higher spectral content, suggesting the neural effect may partially reflect stimulus differences rather than purely familiarity-driven top-down modulation.

results.result: Music with easy-to-perceive beats elicited stronger neural synchronization as measured by TRF correlations.
results.evaluation: Statistical support is provided (C56: t(33)=-2.43, pFDR=0.03, re=0.44) based on subjective ratings. However, similar to familiarity, the stimulus FFT analysis (C57) shows that easier-to-perceive beats had higher spectral content, creating a confound between perceptual ease and acoustic properties. The causal direction (does beat salience enhance synchronization, or do stronger acoustic features drive both?) remains ambiguous.

results.result: TRF and RCA analysis approaches produced convergent results, with SRCorr significantly predicting TRF correlations across all musical features (R²=0.28-0.76), suggesting both methods capture similar aspects of neural synchronization despite methodological differences.
results.evaluation: Strong statistical support across all features (C49: p<1e-14 to <1e-15) with substantial effect sizes. The finding that first harmonic SRCoh better predicts TRF correlations than stimulation tempo (C51, C120) is informative about the frequency content captured by broadband TRF analysis. However, the interpretation that both methods access the same neural mechanisms (C124-C125) is speculative—correlation between measures doesn't establish they reflect identical physiological processes.

results.result: Musical enjoyment did not significantly affect neural synchronization strength (TRF correlations), though the effect approached significance (p=0.06).
results.evaluation: The null finding is appropriately reported with exact p-value (C54: t(33)=1.91, pFDR=0.06, re=0.36). However, the study may be underpowered to detect smaller effects of enjoyment, and the stimulus FFT analysis (C57) shows more enjoyed music had higher spectral content, suggesting a potential confound that could mask or complicate the relationship. The interpretation (C105) appropriately focuses on predictability rather than enjoyment.

results.result: Musical training (Gold-MSI scores) did not correlate with neural synchronization strength, contrasting with prior studies that found musician advantages, possibly due to genre diversity in stimuli and potential confounding of training with familiarity in prior work.
results.evaluation: The null finding is clearly reported (C58: all p>0.2) with adequate sample size (n=34). The authors provide plausible explanations for the discrepancy with prior work (C108-C110), noting their use of diverse genres vs. classical music in prior studies. However, the speculation about confounding in prior studies (C110) is not directly tested. The Gold-MSI may also not capture all relevant aspects of musical expertise for this task.

results.result: Neural synchronization (SRCoh) was stronger at the first harmonic of the stimulation tempo than at the fundamental frequency, likely reflecting synchronization to faster musical elements (notes) in addition to beat rate.
results.evaluation: Strong statistical support across all features (C36: p<0.001-0.01, re=0.56-0.73). The stimulus analysis (C37) shows this pattern is also present in the music itself. The interpretation invoking note-level synchronization (C75-C77) is plausible and supported by prior work (C76), though alternative explanations (1/f slope effects, C78) are also acknowledged. The finding has important implications for interpreting frequency-domain analyses of neural synchronization.

results.result: Spectral flux shared significant mutual information with all other musical features (amplitude envelope, derivative, beat times), with strongest overlap with the derivative (η²=0.45).
results.evaluation: Statistical support is provided for all comparisons (C31: p<1.3e-5 to 1.92e-13). This analysis is critical for interpreting the spectral flux results, as it demonstrates both overlap and unique information. However, mutual information quantifies statistical dependence but doesn't fully characterize the nature of the relationship. The finding that spectral flux shares information with all features supports the interpretation that it's a more comprehensive measure (C44-C45).

results.result: The amount of tempo manipulation applied to music stimuli did not significantly affect neural synchronization (TRF correlations), suggesting the tempo effects reflect genuine neural preferences rather than artifacts of stimulus naturalness.
results.evaluation: The control analysis addresses an important confound (C40: F<0.5, p>0.4), but was only conducted for two tempo conditions (2.25 Hz and 1.5 Hz) due to stimulus constraints. The authors acknowledge this limitation, noting the experiment wasn't designed to fully address this question. While the available data support the interpretation (C72), the limited scope of the control analysis prevents definitive conclusions about all tempo conditions. Additional experiments with balanced tempo manipulation would be needed.

results.result: Behavioral ratings (enjoyment, familiarity, ease of beat tapping) were not significantly affected by tempo manipulation.
results.evaluation: Statistical support is provided (C53: all p>0.08, η²=0.02-0.05). This finding is important for interpreting the neural tempo effects, as it suggests the neural preference for slower tempi is not simply driven by subjective preference differences. However, the lack of tempo effects on ratings could also reflect insensitivity of the rating scales or that the tempo range tested didn't span participants' preference boundaries.

results.result: The first reliable component from RCA exhibited an auditory topography, validating its use for analyzing auditory neural responses.
results.evaluation: The claim is supported by visual inspection of the topography (Figure 2A). This is a standard validation step for RCA analysis. However, no quantitative metrics of topography are provided, and the determination appears to be based on qualitative assessment. The topography is consistent with auditory sources, supporting the validity of subsequent analyses using RC1.

results.result: The study included 34 participants (from 37 recruited) after exclusions, all German speakers with mostly normal hearing, providing adequate power for within-subject comparisons.
results.evaluation: Sample characteristics are clearly documented (C126-C131). The exclusion criteria are appropriate (C127). Power analysis indicated n=24 was sufficient for within-subject comparisons, and the final n=34 exceeds this. However, for correlation analyses, the target was n=32, so the study is at the lower bound of adequate power for those analyses. Ethical approval is documented (C132).

results.result: The stimulus set comprised 703 tempo-manipulated segments from 72 original musical pieces across diverse genres, with 4-4.6 minutes of music per tempo condition per participant, presented at individually calibrated loudness levels.
results.evaluation: Stimulus preparation is thoroughly documented (C133-C137). The use of diverse genres and instrumental versions is appropriate for generalizability. The tempo manipulation procedure (C136) and quality control (C137) are described. The experimental design with four stimulus lists (C138-C139) helps distribute stimuli across tempi while maintaining adequate duration per condition. Individual loudness calibration (C140) controls for hearing sensitivity differences. This is a well-designed stimulus set.
